lessons.title: Antithesis as judgement: Johnson’s Preface to Shakespeare and the sentence that weighs a poet
lessons.explanation: Johnson’s Preface to Shakespeare (1765) is the most influential short piece of judging prose in English, and its authority rests less on its opinions than on the shape of its sentences. It opens its argument with a restriction: “Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature.” Read the grammar rather than the sentiment. The word “but” here means “except”, so the sentence does not praise generality; it makes durability of pleasure the test and then narrows the class of writing that can pass it. The same word “please” appears twice, which converts a vague compliment into a measurable claim: many readers, over long time. Two paragraphs later the criterion is applied to a person: “Shakespeare is above all writers, at least above all modern writers, the poet of nature; the poet that holds up to his readers a faithful mirrour of manners and of life.” The clause “at least above all modern writers” is a concession inserted inside a superlative, and it is typical of the Preface’s method. Johnson rarely asserts without immediately marking the limit of the assertion, and the limit is what makes the assertion usable. Lesson 67 introduced Johnson as an adverse critic of Milton’s “Lycidas”; this lesson reads the prose in which the adverse judgement is manufactured, and lesson 63 established his objection to the metaphysical conceit, which will return as the second example below.
lessons.example: Follow one paragraph in the Preface from concession to rule. Johnson has just praised Shakespeare’s characters as “the genuine progeny of common humanity” and then turns to the objections: “His adherence to general nature has exposed him to the censure of criticks, who form their judgments upon narrower principles. Dennis and Rhymer think his Romans not sufficiently Roman; and Voltaire censures his kings as not completely royal.” The names are not decoration; they are witnesses for the prosecution, each with a specific charge, and the charges are all of the same kind, that Shakespeare’s persons are insufficiently local. The answer arrives in a single monosyllable: “But Shakespeare always makes nature predominate over accident.” Johnson does not deny the local inaccuracy; he reclassifies it. “Nature” and “accident” are the terms of the antithesis, and the sentence concedes everything the critics said while withdrawing the standard by which it counted as a fault. The same manoeuvre, at larger scale, governs the famous defence of the mixed drama. Johnson grants the premise outright: “That this is a practice contrary to the rules of criticism will be readily allowed”. Then comes the hinge: “but there is always an appeal open from criticism to nature. The end of writing is to instruct; the end of poetry is to instruct by pleasing.” The word “appeal” is juridical, and it implies a hierarchy of courts: criticism is a lower court and nature is the court of appeal. The next sentence then supplies the rule that decides the case, and it does so in the form of two parallel definitions whose second term absorbs the first, since poetry instructs by pleasing rather than instead of pleasing. Remove the balance and you get assertion; keep the balance and you get an argument with its jurisdiction stated.
lessons.question: A student paraphrases “there is always an appeal open from criticism to nature” as “Johnson thinks critics should relax”. Why is the paraphrase inadequate?
lessons.answer: It drops the jurisdictional claim: the sentence asserts that criticism is subordinate to a higher standard, which is why an admitted breach of the rules can be defended rather than excused
lessons.distractor: It is inadequate because Johnson was himself a critic and therefore could not consistently appeal against criticism
lessons.correction: The institutional objection misses the point, since the appeal is from criticism to nature, not from all judgement to none. What the paraphrase loses is the hierarchy: “appeal” makes the rules provisional and the standard final. A student who writes “critics should relax” has kept the tone and discarded the argument, which is the commonest way in which Johnson’s prose is admired and not read.

depth.definitions: Antithesis is the setting of two terms against each other in balanced clauses so that the relation between them carries meaning. A concessive is a clause that grants an opponent’s point before answering it. Periodic syntax suspends the main assertion until the end of the sentence; running syntax completes clauses as it goes. Jurisdiction, in this lesson’s legal metaphor, is the authority of a court to decide a case. Generality and accident are Johnson’s paired terms: what belongs to human nature everywhere against what belongs to a particular place or fashion. Prerequisites: lesson 67, which introduces Johnson as an adverse critic, and lesson 63, which introduces his objection to the metaphysical conceit.
depth.mechanism: The Preface works by a three-step procedure that can be marked in almost every paragraph. First a criterion is stated as a restriction, so that it excludes as well as includes. Then the criterion is applied to a named case with named opponents, which supplies the friction an argument needs. Then a concessive “but” converts the opponent’s evidence into support for a larger rule. The balance of the clauses is not ornament laid on top of this procedure; it is how the relation between the terms becomes visible, since a pair of clauses invites the reader to ask which term governs the other. The limitation to state is that the procedure can defend any conclusion, including a wrong one, because “nature” is a standard Johnson never defines operationally. He tells us that Shakespeare mirrors manners and life, not how a reader would tell a true mirror from a flattering one, and that gap is where later critics, Hazlitt among them, put their objection.
depth.secondExample: The same machinery, used to convict rather than to defend, appears in the Life of Cowley (1779). Johnson defines metaphysical wit as “a kind of discordia concors; a combination of dissimilar images, or discovery of occult resemblances in things apparently unlike”, then delivers the verdict in one of the most quoted sentences in English criticism: “The most heterogeneous ideas are yoked by violence together”. The figure is agricultural, the yoke being what joins oxen that do not wish to be joined, and it is an antithesis compressed into a metaphor. The sentence that follows completes the judgement with a clause pair: “the reader commonly thinks his improvement dearly bought, and though he sometimes admires, is seldom pleased.” Notice that “pleased” is the criterion from the Preface, now used as an instrument of condemnation, and that “admires” is granted rather than denied. The difference between this case and the defence of Shakespeare is instructive: in the Preface the balance defends a writer against critics, here it convicts a school of poets, and in both the verdict depends on which term of the pair is allowed to govern.
depth.mistake: The usual error is to read Johnson’s parallel clauses as a mannerism, the “Johnsonian balance”, and therefore as evidence of confidence or pomposity. Diagnose it by asking of each pair what the second clause does that the first could not: in “The end of writing is to instruct; the end of poetry is to instruct by pleasing”, the second clause restricts the first, and in “though he sometimes admires, is seldom pleased” the second clause reverses the weight of the first. Where a pair genuinely adds nothing, the charge of mannerism holds, and Hazlitt made exactly that charge, so the test is worth applying rather than assuming. A second error is to treat “nature” as a self-evident standard; it is a placeholder whose content the argument must supply, and Johnson supplies it through examples rather than definitions.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take the paragraph beginning “That this is a practice contrary to the rules of criticism” and do three things. Mark every clause pair with brackets. Rewrite the paragraph as plain sequential prose, one assertion per sentence, keeping the content and dropping the balance. Then write 150 words on what the rewrite loses. Worked model, checked against the task: “The rewrite reads: Shakespeare breaks the rules; the rules are not final; nature is; writing should instruct; poetry should please while instructing; therefore mixed drama is legitimate. What vanishes is the subordination: in the original the defence of mixing arrives as the conclusion of a definition, so the reader is led to it rather than told it. The paraphrase also loses the legal metaphor, which had made the rules provisional without abolishing them.” A satisfactory answer marks the pairs; an excellent one names a pair whose second term does no work and says so.
depth.summary: Johnson’s judgements are carried by sentence structure: a criterion stated as a restriction, opponents named, a concessive that converts their evidence into a larger rule. The balance is the argument, and the argument’s weak point is the undefined standard of nature.

lessons.title: Irony in the subordinate clause: Gibbon on the progress of Christianity, chapter XV
lessons.explanation: The fifteenth chapter of the Decline and Fall (1776) begins with a sentence that appears to promise neutrality and quietly rigs the enquiry: “A candid but rational inquiry into the progress and establishment of Christianity may be considered as a very essential part of the history of the Roman empire.” The pair “candid but rational” looks like two virtues; in fact the second term governs, and it tells the reader in advance what kind of explanation will count. What follows is one of the great long sentences of English prose: “While that great body was invaded by open violence, or undermined by slow decay, a pure and humble religion gently insinuated itself into the minds of men, grew up in silence and obscurity, derived new vigor from opposition, and finally erected the triumphant banner of the Cross on the ruins of the Capitol.” Four verbs carry the whole history, and each is loaded. “Insinuated” is not a neutral word for entering; “obscurity” is not a compliment in a history written by an Enlightenment sceptic; and “erected the triumphant banner” ends a sentence about humility in the vocabulary of military conquest. Nothing here is a false statement. Everything here is a selection. That is the mechanism of Gibbonian irony: the reader is given sentences an orthodox believer could assent to, arranged so that assent becomes embarrassing.
lessons.example: Watch the famous withdrawal at the end of the chapter’s opening survey. Gibbon asks by what means the faith obtained “so remarkable a victory over the established religions of the earth”, and answers: “To this inquiry, an obvious but satisfactory answer may be returned; that it was owing to the convincing evidence of the doctrine itself, and to the ruling providence of its great Author.” The sentence has just given the pious explanation, in full, with the two causes an eighteenth-century clergyman would name. Then the next sentence removes the ground: “But as truth and reason seldom find so favorable a reception in the world, and as the wisdom of Providence frequently condescends to use the passions of the human heart, and the general circumstances of mankind, as instruments to execute its purpose, we may still be permitted, though with becoming submission, to ask, not indeed what were the first, but what were the secondary causes of the rapid growth of the Christian church.” Every clause in this sentence is doing work. “Seldom find so favorable a reception” concedes human depravity while implying that the evidence did not in fact convince anyone. “Condescends to use the passions” converts providence into a manager of vices. “Permitted” and “becoming submission” mark the writer as a man under surveillance. And “not indeed what were the first, but what were the secondary causes” is the technical move on which the whole chapter turns: admit the first cause, then explain everything by the second, and the first becomes a formality. The irony is deniable by design, which is why the chapter provoked pamphlets rather than prosecutions.
lessons.question: Gibbon writes that “an obvious but satisfactory answer may be returned” and then answers with providence. What is the sentence doing?
lessons.answer: It grants the orthodox explanation in order to withdraw its explanatory force in the next sentence, where the enquiry is redirected from first to secondary causes
lessons.distractor: It endorses the orthodox explanation, since “satisfactory” is a word of approval and the sentence stands at the head of the chapter’s argument
lessons.correction: The word “obvious” is the tell: in Gibbon’s vocabulary an obvious answer is the one everybody gives, not the one that explains. The withdrawal in the next sentence, with its “But as truth and reason seldom find so favorable a reception”, is what turns the grant into a gesture. A reader who takes “satisfactory” at face value has read the sentence in isolation, which is the standard way of missing irony in prose that never states its conclusion.

depth.definitions: Irony is a mode in which the stated sense is qualified or reversed by context, tone or structure, without the statement being literally false. A first cause is a primary or ultimate explanation; secondary causes are the intermediate natural means. Providence is divine government of events. Insinuate means to enter by stealth, and the word carries suspicion in eighteenth-century usage. A hedge is a phrase that limits the writer’s commitment, such as “with becoming submission”. Prerequisites: lesson 35 on irony as a sentence-level effect, lesson 61 on reading a single word against its context, and lesson 71 on the concessive as an instrument of judgement.
depth.mechanism: Gibbon’s irony is built from four devices, all of them syntactical rather than tonal. The concessive “but” grants and then withdraws, as in Johnson, except that Gibbon never names the standard by which the withdrawal is justified. Agentless constructions hide who acts: the faith “obtained” a victory, no one is said to have been convinced. Loaded adjectives sit inside apparently neutral descriptions, so that “obscurity” and “insinuated” carry the judgement while the grammar stays flat. And the disciplinary frame, first causes versus secondary causes, allows a naturalistic account to proceed while orthodoxy is formally untouched. The limit of the method is that irony of this kind cannot be proved by quotation alone. It can be argued from the arrangement of sentences, from the residue of unassimilated details, and from reception, that is, from readers who detected it and objected. Two such readers are available: William Paley, whose exasperated question “Who can refute a sneer?” became the standard contemporary summary, and Milman, the nineteenth-century editor whose note is printed at the foot of this very chapter.
depth.secondExample: Set Gibbon’s hinge beside Johnson’s and the difference in function becomes visible. Johnson writes “But Shakespeare always makes nature predominate over accident”: the “but” is an adjudication, and it names the court that decides. Gibbon writes “But as truth and reason seldom find so favorable a reception in the world”: the “but” is an insinuation, and it names no court at all, only a disappointing fact about audiences. Johnson tells the reader what the standard is; Gibbon lets the reader infer that the standard has just been abandoned. The same grammatical joint, therefore, can either settle an argument or dissolve one, and the test is whether the clause after the “but” identifies an authority. Where it does, the sentence judges; where it merely describes a condition, the sentence manoeuvres. This is the distinction that separates argumentative prose from ironic prose, and it is more reliable than any impression of tone.
depth.mistake: Two opposite errors are common, and both come from reading one sentence instead of a paragraph. The first takes the pious sentences as Gibbon’s position, producing a devout historian who wrote two inexplicable chapters. The second takes the irony as open declaration, producing an atheist tract that says what it never says. Diagnose either by asking what the text asserts and what it merely arranges: Gibbon never writes that Christianity was false, and he never writes that providence explained anything. A third, subtler error is to treat the irony as a secret code, so that any sentence can be reversed at will. That makes interpretation unfalsifiable; the discipline is to point to the arrangement, the loaded adjective, the withdrawn explanation, and to name the readers who responded to it.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: mark the first eight hundred words of chapter XV in three colours, one for sentences stating an orthodox explanation, one for sentences withdrawing or qualifying it, one for sentences offering a natural cause. Then write 150 words answering a single question: does the chapter ever assert a conclusion, or does it only arrange material so that the reader draws one? Model response, self-reviewed: “The chapter asserts no conclusion about the truth of Christianity. It asserts a method, the enquiry into secondary causes, and it apologises for the method with ‘becoming submission’. The natural causes it lists, such as the promise of a future life and the union of the faithful, are offered as sufficient explanations of growth, not as refutations of doctrine. The reader who concludes that doctrine is explained away has supplied the inference the prose declines to state, which is what the arrangement was for.” A satisfactory answer marks the three kinds; an excellent one notes a sentence that could belong to either colour and says why it is undecidable.
depth.summary: Gibbon’s irony lives in arrangement, not assertion: a grant, a withdrawal, an agentless verb, a loaded adjective. Because it never states its conclusion, the evidence for it must come from structure and from the readers who objected.

lessons.title: Anaphora, address and the price of freedom: Paine’s American Crisis, No. I
lessons.explanation: Paine’s first Crisis was printed in the Pennsylvania Journal on 19 December 1776, during Washington’s retreat across the Delaware, and its opening is the most quoted paragraph of American revolutionary prose: “THESE are the times that try men’s souls. The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.” The capitalised first word is a printer’s emphasis of the kind eighteenth-century compositors used for an opening, so it cannot by itself prove urgency; what proves design is the sequence. A maxim states a shared condition, a pair of coined types names the people who will fail, a concessive “but” turns to those who will not, and a reward clause attaches a price to conduct. The paragraph continues in the same manufactured idiom: “Tyranny, like hell, is not easily conquered; yet we have this consolation with us, that the harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph. What we obtain too cheap, we esteem too lightly: it is dearness only that gives every thing its value.” That last sentence is a theory of value in the middle of a battle report, and it is the argument the whole pamphlet needs: if difficulty is what makes freedom worth having, then the current defeats are evidence for the cause rather than against it. Conway’s preface adds a detail about performance that matters for reading the rhythm: it was, he writes, “written during the retreat of Washington across the Delaware, and by order of the Commander was read to groups of his dispirited and suffering soldiers”, and its opening sentence was “adopted as the watchword of the movement on Trenton”. That is a claim by an editor rather than a document, and Conway says the effect was attested by Washington and Franklin; treat it as reception evidence of the kind lesson 72 used for Gibbon.
lessons.example: Read the paragraph as a machine for producing consent. Clause one establishes the moment (“these times”) and the stake (“souls”), which raises the register above politics. Clause two introduces two compounds, “summer soldier” and “sunshine patriot”, and each does the same trick: it takes a pleasant seasonal word and attaches it to a martial or civic noun, so that a whole class of unreliable men is created and named in six syllables. The alliteration is not decoration; it makes the types memorable and therefore usable as insults in a tavern. Then “but” pivots, and the sentence rewards the remainder with “the love and thanks of man and woman”, a phrase whose oddity is worth noticing: not “of their country”, which would be abstract, but of men and women, which is concrete and distributed. The next sentence compares tyranny to hell, which licenses the inference that the difficulty is not accidental, and then converts that inference into consolation through a comparative construction, “the harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph”. The paragraph closes with a maxim about price, and the maxim has a hidden premise: value is conferred by cost. Once that premise is accepted, retreat becomes not merely dishonourable but economically irrational, since the thing obtained cheaply is worth little. Paine does not need to argue the premise; he states it as proverbial wisdom, which is what proverbs are for.
lessons.question: A student says the paragraph persuades by emotion and offers the coined phrase “summer soldier” as an example of emotive language. What is the more accurate account?
lessons.answer: The phrase is a definition in miniature: it creates a category of unreliable patriot and thereby gives the audience a test by which to judge themselves and their neighbours
lessons.distractor: The phrase is emotive because it uses seasonal imagery, and imagery appeals to feeling rather than to judgement
lessons.correction: Imagery can carry judgement, and here it carries a criterion. “Summer soldier” is a compound noun with the grammar of a class term, like “fair-weather friend”; once it exists, a reader can ask whether the description fits. Calling it emotive names the effect and skips the operation, which is categorisation. The same is true of the price maxim: it looks like feeling about hardship and is actually an argument about value.

depth.definitions: Anaphora is the repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses. A maxim is a short general statement offered as received wisdom. A concessive turns from an admitted point to a counter-claim, usually on “but” or “yet”. A compound epithet joins two words into one descriptive unit, as in “sunshine patriot”. Register is the level of formality a text adopts. A pamphlet is a short, cheap, unbound printed work designed for immediate circulation, which is the physical form of the Crisis. Prerequisites: lesson 71 on the concessive as an instrument of judgement, and lesson 64 on stress and rhythm, which supplies the vocabulary for the paragraph’s beat.
depth.mechanism: Three devices cooperate. The maxim supplies a premise the audience already holds, so that the argument begins from agreement rather than from contest. The coined type converts a general warning into a usable social category, and categories can be applied by readers to themselves and to others. The price metaphor converts a moral demand into an exchange, which is the idiom of a commercial readership: freedom has a price, and what is bought cheaply is valued lightly. Around these sits the rhythm, short declaratives after long suspensions, with the colon and semicolon doing the work of beats. What the devices cannot do is guarantee their own premises: a maxim’s authority is borrowed, not earned, and a coined type can be turned against its maker. Both devices depend on the audience sharing the values the pamphlet assumes. That is why the Crisis was effective in 1776 among people already committed to independence and ineffective as an argument to loyalists, who could reply that the “sunshine patriot” was the man who changed sides for popularity.
depth.secondExample: The editor’s preface to the Conway edition records that the thirteenth and last Crisis, printed in April 1783, “opens with the words, ‘The times that tried men’s souls are over.’” Set the two sentences side by side and the technique becomes visible as technique. The first is present tense, addressed to a “we” under threat, and built on a maxim about the soul; the second is past tense, closes the series, and depends entirely on the reader’s memory of the first. Nothing in the later sentence argues; it collects. The pair shows a formula being converted from a summons into a monument, which is what happens to successful political prose, and it also shows why dating matters: the same words mean opposite things depending on whether the war is being lost or concluded. A student who reads the Crisis as a timeless statement about courage will miss that the second sentence is a farewell to the device.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is the Romantic one: treating the opening as unrevised feeling, “dashed off in a crisis”, and therefore as evidence of sincerity rather than craft. Its mirror image is the debunking error, which finds the craft and concludes that the feeling is fake. Both mistakes assume that design and sincerity exclude each other. Diagnose them by pointing to the later reuse of the formula, which no spontaneous utterance would permit, and by pointing to the price maxim, which is a proposition with a premise and can be argued with. A second, narrower error is to read the capitalised “THESE” and “FREEDOM” as authorial emphasis when they are compositor’s convention, which shows how easily typography is mistaken for tone.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: reconstruct the paragraph’s implicit argument in four numbered steps, then rewrite the paragraph for a modern reader, keeping the argument and dropping the coinages and the price metaphor. Finish with 120 words on what the rewrite loses. A model answer, self-reviewed: “1. The present moment tests character. 2. Some people will fail the test when it costs them comfort. 3. Those who do not fail earn the gratitude of ordinary people. 4. Difficulty is what makes a thing valuable, so the current difficulty is evidence of value. The rewrite is clearer and weaker: without the coined types the reader has no label to apply to a neighbour, and without the price metaphor the argument loses its appeal to a commercial audience’s instinct that cheap goods are worthless.” A satisfactory attempt gets the steps; an excellent one notices that step 4 is asserted rather than argued.
depth.summary: Paine’s paragraph persuades by manufacturing categories and premises: a maxim everyone grants, two coined types everyone can apply, a concessive that rewards the loyal, and a price metaphor that makes hardship evidence of value. The design is compatible with sincerity, and the later reuse of the formula proves the design.

lessons.title: The essayist’s persona: Hazlitt’s ‘On Going a Journey’ and the ‘I’ that is not the man
lessons.explanation: Hazlitt’s ‘On Going a Journey’ opens with a preference dressed as a general truth: “One of the pleasantest things in the world is going a journey; but I like to go by myself. I can enjoy society in a room; but out of doors, nature is company enough for me. I am then never less alone than when alone.” Three sentences, three first-person verbs, and a reader feels a temperament has been disclosed. The feeling is an effect of craft. The essay was published in The New Monthly Magazine in 1822 under the heading “Table Talk, No. 1”, as the annotated edition of Hazlitt’s collected works records, and that heading tells you what kind of “I” is on offer: a talker’s, produced for a periodical, in a series, for readers who expect a performance of candour rather than a confession. The third sentence confirms the point, since “never less alone than when alone” is not Hazlitt’s invention but a classical sententia that he has Englished, and the annotated edition identifies the verse quotations that follow as Bloomfield, Cowper and Milton. The essay’s solitude is a solitude assembled from other people’s sentences, which is exactly what a persona is.
lessons.example: Read the second paragraph as a demonstration. “I cannot see the wit of walking and talking at the same time. When I am in the country I wish to vegetate like the country. I am not for criticising hedge-rows and black cattle. I go out of town in order to forget the town and all that is in it.” The syntax is plain, the vocabulary is largely monosyllabic, and each sentence asserts a preference rather than arguing one, which produces the impression of a man thinking aloud. Then comes the sentence that gives the game away, because it is a quotation doing the work of a conviction: “I like solitude, when I give myself up to it, for the sake of solitude; nor do I ask for / A friend in my retreat, / Whom I may whisper solitude is sweet.” The verse is Cowper’s, as the editor’s note records, and the “I” who does not ask for a friend is therefore speaking partly in Cowper’s words. Hazlitt’s theory, set out in ‘On Familiar Style’ in the same collection, is that “to write a genuine familiar or truly English style is to write as any one would speak in common conversation who had a thorough command and choice of words”, and that the style “is not to take the first word that offers, but the best word in common use”. That is a demanding standard, and the essay meets it: the words are common, the choices are exact, and the ease is produced by selection. The persona is the man who has made those choices, which is not the same thing as the man who took the walk.
lessons.question: A reader argues that because ‘On Going a Journey’ is written in the first person and reports preferences, it is a straightforward record of Hazlitt’s habits. What is the strongest objection?
lessons.answer: The essay is a periodical performance built from borrowed verse, received sententiae and selected detail, so its “I” is a constructed voice whose consistency is an artistic effect rather than a biographical report
lessons.distractor: The objection fails because Romantic essayists were required by their publishers to write only about their own lives
lessons.correction: There was no such requirement, and the essay’s own publication history contradicts the simplicity the reader assumes: it appeared as the first number of a magazine series, which is a slot for a performance. The evidence against the autobiographical reading is internal as well as external, since the most intimate sentences are quotations from Cowper and Milton. A persona can be sincere and still be made; the question to ask is what the voice insists on and what it leaves out.

depth.definitions: Persona is the voice a writer assumes, distinct from the historical author. The familiar essay is a short prose form that cultivates intimacy, digression and a talkative first person. A sententia is a quoted maxim or proverbial sentence. Antithesis sets two terms against each other in balanced clauses. A periodical is a magazine or review, and the essay’s first appearance in one is part of its meaning. Prerequisites: lesson 54 on Montaigne’s essay as a form, and lesson 71 on Johnson’s antithesis, which is the style Hazlitt attacks here.
depth.mechanism: The persona is built by four means, all visible in the opening paragraphs. First-person present-tense preferences create the illusion of a mind in act, since the present tense reports inclination rather than event. Plain diction and short clauses produce the sound of conversation, which the theory in ‘On Familiar Style’ explicitly aims at. Borrowed verse imports authority and sentiment without the writer having to assert them in his own person, so that the “I” speaks in a composite voice. And antithesis organises the preferences into a character, since a man who enjoys society in a room but not out of doors has been given a shape. The constraint is that this method cannot establish sincerity, only consistency, and consistency can be manufactured. That is why the biographical question is unanswerable from the essay alone, and why the interesting questions are formal: which preferences recur, which are contradicted, and which quotations the voice chooses to inhabit.
depth.secondExample: Hazlitt’s attack on Johnson in ‘On Familiar Style’ supplies the unit’s pivot. He writes that “The reason why I object to Dr. Johnson’s style is that there is no discrimination, no selection, no variety in it”, and that Johnson uses “none but ‘tall, opaque words’” taken from “the first row of the rubric”. The charge is precise: balance without discrimination, symmetry that does not register a difference. Yet the accusing sentence is itself a triad with a repeated frame, “no discrimination, no selection, no variety”, which is a Johnsonian figure turned against Johnson. That is not hypocrisy; it is the strongest evidence for Hazlitt’s position, because it shows that the device is neutral and that the question is what it carries. Applied back to lesson 71, the test is functional: in Johnson’s “The end of writing is to instruct; the end of poetry is to instruct by pleasing” the second clause narrows the first, while in Hazlitt’s triad each item adds a distinct accusation, discrimination being about choice, selection about range, variety about monotony.
depth.mistake: The usual error is to read the essay’s “I” as autobiography, and its mirror is to conclude that because the voice is constructed, the essay is insincere or merely decorative. Both treat persona as a matter of truthfulness. Diagnose the first by pointing to the borrowed verse and the magazine slot; diagnose the second by pointing out that a constructed voice can still make claims that are true or false about the world, such as the claim that travelling alone is pleasanter than travelling with a companion. A further error is to suppose that the theory in ‘On Familiar Style’ and the practice in ‘On Going a Journey’ must agree; the useful exercise is to test one against the other, since Hazlitt’s own prose contains words, such as “vegetate” and “impertinence”, that a strict application of his rule would have to defend.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take the essay’s first three paragraphs and make three columns, one for first-person assertions, one for quotations and allusions, one for antitheses. Then apply Hazlitt’s own rule from ‘On Familiar Style’ and write 150 words on whether the passage would pass it. Model response, self-reviewed: “The first column is almost entirely present-tense preference, which is what produces the talkative effect. The second column contains a classical sententia and at least three verse quotations, so the voice is composite at the points where it sounds most personal. The third column shows the essay’s structure: room against outdoors, town against country, company against solitude. On Hazlitt’s rule the passage passes, since the words are common and exactly chosen; but the rule does not cover the quotations, which are neither common nor conversational, so his theory accounts for the diction and not for the ventriloquism.” A satisfactory answer fills the columns; an excellent one finds a sentence that fails the rule.
depth.summary: Hazlitt’s familiar style is a designed intimacy: plain diction, present-tense preference, borrowed verse and antithesis produce a persona rather than a report. His attack on Johnson shows that the device is neutral and that the question is always what a balance carries.

lessons.title: The frame that judges: Thackeray’s ‘Before the Curtain’ and the manager who will not stay out
lessons.explanation: Vanity Fair opens with a device rather than a scene. “Before the Curtain” presents a speaker who describes himself in the third person: “As the manager of the Performance sits before the curtain on the boards and looks into the Fair, a feeling of profound melancholy comes over him in his survey of the bustling place.” The sentence is a stage direction for a novel, and it installs three positions at once: a fair, a manager who watches it, and a reader placed where the manager sits. The catalogue that follows is deliberately indiscriminate, “eating and drinking, making love and jilting, laughing and the contrary, smoking, cheating, fighting, dancing and fiddling”, and it includes the observers as part of the show, since there are “policemen on the look-out” and “quacks (OTHER quacks, plague take them!) bawling in front of their booths”. The parenthesis is the first crack in the managerial voice: a manager who says “other quacks” has admitted that he is one of them. The title alludes to Bunyan’s Vanity Fair in The Pilgrim’s Progress, a fair of merchandise and vanity that Christian and Faithful pass through in the first part, and Thackeray’s version keeps the commercial sense: this is a place where everything, including reputation, is for sale. Lesson 34 examined frames that filter testimony in Wuthering Heights; here the frame is printed before chapter one and belongs to the novel’s paratext, which is why editions can remove it and believe they have lost nothing.
lessons.example: Track the pronouns through the preface, because the pronouns are the argument. It begins in the third person, with “the manager” and “him”, which keeps the speaker at a distance and makes him sound like a fixture of the theatre rather than an author. Then the essay slides into judgement in the first person: “A man with a reflective turn of mind, walking through an exhibition of this sort, will not be oppressed, I take it, by his own or other people’s hilarity.” “I take it” is a small phrase doing large work, since it converts a general observation into a personal opinion while pretending to be a hedge. The catalogue of touching details that follows, “a pretty child looking at a gingerbread stall; a pretty girl blushing whilst her lover talks to her and chooses her fairing”, is offered as evidence for the melancholy, and the reader is invited to share the survey. By the close of the novel the same voice addresses the reader directly and as a child: “Ah! Vanitas Vanitatum! which of us is happy in this world? Which of us has his desire? or, having it, is satisfied? come, children, let us shut up the box and the puppets, for our play is played out.” The puppets were introduced at the beginning and are packed away at the end, so the frame encloses the whole fiction and fixes its duration. The word “children” is the final turn of the screw: the reader has been watching the show, and is now told that the show was for him and that he is a child.
lessons.question: An editor proposes to drop “Before the Curtain” because it delays the story and states opinions the novel later complicates. What is the best objection?
lessons.answer: The preface installs the puppet-show frame that the final chapter closes, so removing it breaks a device that positions the reader as an audience and makes the characters performers
lessons.distractor: The preface must stay because an author’s preface is part of the text and editors have no business altering texts
lessons.correction: The conservative objection is true as a general principle but it does not say what is at stake here. The frame is load-bearing: the manager, the box and the puppets appear at both ends of the novel, and the address to “children” at the close depends on the audience having been constituted at the start. An editor may abridge, but should record the cost, and the cost in this case is the novel’s stated model of what its people are.

depth.definitions: A frame is a device that encloses a narrative, supplying a speaker, an occasion or an audience for the story. A paratext is material attached to a text but outside its main body, such as a preface, title page or dedication. A persona is the voice a writer assumes. Direct address is speech to a “you” or an imperative to the reader. Vanity Fair in Bunyan is a town fair of merchandise and vanity in The Pilgrim’s Progress. Prerequisites: lesson 34 on frames and interested testimony, lesson 35 on irony, and lesson 74 on the essayistic persona, which supplies the vocabulary for a constructed voice.
depth.mechanism: The frame works by distributing judgement across three grammatical persons. Third person establishes the manager as a role rather than a man, which gives him institutional authority. First person in “I take it” makes him a participant, and participation compromises the authority that the role supplied. Second person, in the imperative “Look at the faces of the actors and buffoons”, transfers the act of judgement to the reader, who is now the one looking. The puppet metaphor then supplies the ontology: if the characters are puppets, their struggles are performances, and the reader’s sympathy is an audience’s sympathy. The limitation to state is that a puppet show implies a puppeteer, and the novel never decides whether the manager controls the strings or merely watches. That undecided point is productive, because it lets Thackeray moralise without claiming omniscience, and it is why the narrator can later insist, in the same voice, that his history is one “of which every word is true”.
depth.secondExample: Near the end of the novel the narrator performs the opposite manoeuvre with the same apparatus. Having shown the characters in Pumpernickel, he writes: “It was on this very tour that I, the present writer of a history of which every word is true, had the pleasure to see them first and to make their acquaintance.” The claim is a joke that the reader has been prepared for by two years of managerial commentary, and Zelma Catalan reads it as a retreat: with the narrator’s superior omniscience under threat, he refashions the stage set into a world where he is trustworthy because he knows the characters personally. Set the two passages side by side and the frame’s double function becomes clear. The opening uses the theatre to place the reader as judge; the closing uses the theatre to authenticate the report as eyewitness. A device introduced to produce detachment ends by producing credence, and the shift is exactly what an attentive reader of the preface should expect from a manager who has already admitted to being one of the quacks.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is to treat the manager’s opinions as Thackeray’s own, and therefore to read the preface as a moral essay appended to a novel. The opposite error is to treat the frame as a mere convention of nineteenth-century fiction, which licenses skipping it. To diagnose the first, notice that the manager is described in the third person and compromised by his own parenthesis. To diagnose the second, notice that the closing chapter returns to the metaphor, which no mere convention would require. One further error is to assume that because the narrator is unreliable the novel has no judgements; the frame’s function is precisely to make judgement possible without guaranteeing the judge.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: mark every pronoun in “Before the Curtain” that refers to the speaker, classify each as third person, first person or implied second person, and then write 150 words on where the reader is positioned at the end of the preface. Model answer, checked line by line: “The speaker is ‘the manager’ and ‘him’ for the first paragraph, which puts him on the same level as the fair he surveys. ‘I take it’ enters in the second paragraph and makes the survey an opinion. The imperative ‘Look at the faces’ and the closing ‘come, children’ put the reader in the audience and then in the position of a child being led out of the theatre. The reader is therefore not a judge but a spectator who has been told what to feel and then told that the show is over.” A satisfactory answer marks the pronouns; an excellent one explains why the third-person opening makes the later first person feel like a confidence.
depth.summary: Thackeray’s preface is a working part of the novel: a manager installed in the third person, compromised by his own parenthesis, who shifts into the first person, hands judgement to the reader, and returns at the close to pack away the puppets and address the audience as children.

questions.prompt: A student annotating Johnson’s Preface to Shakespeare marks the sentence “there is always an appeal open from criticism to nature” as a polite concession and moves on. A tutor asks what the sentence is doing in its paragraph, which has just granted that Shakespeare’s mixed drama breaks the rules. Which description of the sentence’s work is best supported?
questions.answer: It is the hinge of the argument: having conceded the breach of rule, Johnson transfers authority from critics to nature, so the concession becomes the ground of a defence rather than an apology
questions.distractor: It is a courteous aside, since Johnson immediately returns to the rules and never mentions nature again in the Preface
questions.correction: The move is structural, not courteous. Johnson has just written that the practice is “contrary to the rules of criticism”, and the appeal to nature is what converts that admission into a claim about which tribunal has jurisdiction. Reading it as an aside severs the sentence from the two that follow, where the end of writing and the end of poetry are defined in order to license the mingled drama.

questions.prompt: A review describes Gibbon as a straightforwardly devout historian whose fifteenth chapter merely reports the growth of the church, and quotes “a pure and humble religion gently insinuated itself into the minds of men” as evidence of piety. What is wrong with the use of that quotation?
questions.answer: The phrasing is doing ironic work that the review suppresses: the sentence continues into military and botanical figures (“derived new vigor from opposition”, “erected the triumphant banner”), and the chapter’s own “obvious but satisfactory answer” is withdrawn two sentences later
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because an author’s ironic intention cannot be established from prose and quotations must be read literally
questions.correction: The quotation is accurate but truncated at the point where the irony becomes visible. The clause sequence moves from insinuation to growth to military triumph, and the chapter then offers a providential explanation it immediately qualifies with “But as truth and reason seldom find so favorable a reception”. A reader who stops at “gently insinuated” has quoted the set-up and called it the conclusion. Reading irony does not require intention; it requires the rest of the sentence.

questions.prompt: An essay submitted on Paine’s Crisis No. I says the opening is powerful because it is “raw, spontaneous feeling dashed off in a crisis”. The student points to the capitals in “THESE” and “FREEDOM” as marks of unrevised emotion. How should the claim be corrected?
questions.answer: The opening is a designed piece of prose: a maxim in the first sentence, a coined compound (“summer soldier”) that names a social type, a price metaphor, and a pivot on “but”, all of which are repeatable techniques rather than symptoms of haste
questions.distractor: The capitals prove the opposite, since eighteenth-century printers capitalised nouns mechanically and the passage therefore carries no emphasis at all
questions.correction: The capitals are a compositor’s convention, so they cannot establish either spontaneity or emphasis; that is the student’s first error. The larger error is to treat rhetorical design as insincerity or as its absence. The sentence builds a maxim, a type, a consolation and a metaphor in sequence, and Paine reused the formula years later, which is what a technique looks like rather than what a mood looks like.

questions.prompt: A reader concludes from “I like to go by myself” that Hazlitt was a solitary man and that the essay is therefore a reliable record of his habits, while a second reader concludes that because the essay is a performance, nothing in it can be believed. Which assessment of the pair is best?
questions.answer: Both readers mistake a constructed persona for a person or for a lie: the essay builds a speaker by selection and antithesis, and the biographical question is separate from the question of what the persona is made to argue
questions.distractor: The first reader is right, since first-person essays are autobiographical by definition, and the second reader is over-reading
questions.correction: The first-person essay is a form with conventions, not a sworn deposition. Hazlitt selects, exaggerates and borrows sententiae, and he also wrote a separate essay on style that states the theory behind the selection. Persona is not deceit; it is a designed consistency of voice, and the analysable question is which preferences the voice insists on and which it suppresses.

questions.prompt: An editor proposes to cut Thackeray’s “Before the Curtain” from a school edition on the ground that it delays the story and expresses opinions the novel later undermines. Which objection is strongest?
questions.answer: The preface installs the puppet-show frame that the final chapter closes, so cutting it removes the device by which the novel measures its own characters and hands judgement to the reader
questions.distractor: The preface should be kept because prefaces are authorial documents and no editor may alter the contents of a novel
questions.correction: Textual conservatism is not the argument here; the frame is functionally load-bearing. The manager who looks into the fair, the shift into direct address, and the closing instruction to “shut up the box and the puppets” form one device in two places. An edition may abridge, but it should record what the abridgement costs, and in this case the cost is the novel’s stated model of what its characters are.

lessons.title: The chapter as an argument: fog, mud and compound interest in Bleak House, chapter I
lessons.explanation: Bleak House opens without a character. Three fragments establish the scene: “London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather.” Place, legal calendar, climate, in that order, and no human being named. The adjective “implacable” normally belongs to an enemy or a person who will not be appeased, so the weather is introduced as an adversary before anything has happened. What follows accumulates in the same spirit. The mud is “as much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth”, which puts the street in the condition of the deluge; a Megalosaurus, “forty feet long or so”, might be met “waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill”, which puts geological time in a London street; the smoke is “gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun”, which is an image of cosmic extinction applied to a chimney; and the mud is “accumulating at compound interest”, which is a metaphor from finance applied to a pavement. Each figure is exact and each belongs to a different domain, so the passage reads as description while performing an argument: this is a world where natural, legal, geological and financial orders have collapsed into one another. Lesson 39 examined Coketown as setting that argues; this chapter is the strongest Victorian case of the technique, and it achieves it without a single protagonist.
lessons.example: The fog paragraph is the chapter’s engine, and its grammar can be counted. “Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city. Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights.” The anaphora establishes extent, and the prepositions do the surveying, up and down, on and on. Then the fog enters property: “Fog creeping into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales of barges and small boats.” Then it enters bodies: “Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper, down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck.” The movement from geography to possessions to lungs is the argument, and the last clause is the one that matters, because the fog is now an agent that pinches a child. The paragraph then contracts with a triple superlative and a chain of prepositions: “The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the muddy streets are muddiest near that leaden-headed old obstruction”, which is Temple Bar, and then “hard by Temple Bar, in Lincoln’s Inn Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in his High Court of Chancery.” Everything the chapter has spread across a city is gathered into one room, and the institution is placed at the centre of the condition rather than offered as its cause.
lessons.question: A student writes that the fog “symbolises the Court of Chancery” and cites “Fog everywhere” as proof. What is the weakness?
lessons.answer: The repetition establishes pervasiveness, and the symbolic equivalence has to be argued from the chapter’s contraction onto Lincoln’s Inn Hall and from its financial metaphors, not from the anaphora alone
lessons.distractor: The weakness is that fog is a physical fact and physical facts cannot carry meaning in a novel
lessons.correction: Physical facts carry meaning constantly in novels, so the second objection is empty. The real weakness is evidentiary: the anaphora tells you the fog is everywhere, which is a claim about extent, and the identification with Chancery requires the closing movement of the paragraph plus the metaphors that make the law an economy. The difference matters because the weaker version of the claim is defensible and the stronger one needs the whole chapter.

depth.definitions: Anaphora is the repetition of a phrase at the start of successive clauses. Present-tense narration reports events as occurring now, which makes description a standing condition rather than a stage in a plot. A symbol is an image that carries meaning beyond itself. Setting is the place and conditions in which action occurs. Personification attributes agency or feeling to a non-human thing. Prerequisites: lesson 39 on setting as argument, lesson 59 on symbolism that earns its place, and lesson 73 on anaphora in prose.
depth.mechanism: Four devices produce the chapter’s argument. The present tense removes sequence, so the description reads as a permanent state rather than a moment. Anaphora with varied prepositions gives the impression of a survey that is also an inventory, and the inventory moves from landscape to property to bodies, which is an argument about distribution. Rival metaphors from different domains, geology, law, finance and religion, prevent the reader from settling the passage into a single allegory. And the closing contraction, from a city to one room, converts extent into centrality. The limitation is causal: the chapter places Chancery at the heart of the fog and does not say that Chancery produces it. That reticence is the point of a reading by Michael Williams on the Victorian Web, which argues that Dickens names the sources of the smoke and deliberately leaves the fog’s origins unidentified, so that the fog functions as an obfuscation rather than an emanation.
depth.secondExample: The chapter’s second movement turns from weather to procedure, and the difference is instructive. Instead of fog we get the Court: members of the bar “mistily engaged in one of the ten thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words”; solicitors with “bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits, issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly nonsense, piled before them”; and the triple anaphora “well may the court be dim ... well may the fog hang heavy in it ... well may the stained-glass windows lose their colour”. The catalogue of legal instruments is a parody of inventory: in the fog paragraph the inventory was of places and people, here it is of documents, and the effect is to show a system that produces paper instead of decisions. The chapter then generalises: “This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard.” Only here does the chapter make a causal claim, and it makes it by extension, listing effects in every shire rather than asserting a mechanism.
depth.mistake: The standard error is allegorical over-reading: fog equals Chancery equals secrecy equals the novel’s meaning, with each equation asserted rather than argued. Diagnose it by asking what the chapter says about production, since the mud has sources and the fog does not, and by asking which sentences would have to be rewritten if the allegory were the point. The opposite error is to treat the chapter as atmospheric scene-setting, which ignores the movement from city to courtroom and the financial vocabulary that ties the two together. A third error is to quote a modernised text without noticing; a widely used teaching page prints “rolls deified among the tiers of shipping” where the Gutenberg text prints “rolls defiled”, and the difference, whatever its cause, shows why a reader should name the transcription being quoted.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: in the first chapter, underline every verb that attributes agency to the fog, the mud or the smoke, and circle every sentence that names a human producer of either. Close with 150 words on whether the chapter attributes cause, and to whom. Model response, self-reviewed: “The fog creeps, lies, hovers, droops and pinches; the mud accumulates; the smoke lowers. Almost no sentence names a producer, and where production is named it is the Chancellor and the lawyers who produce paper. The chapter therefore attributes effects everywhere and causes almost nowhere, which is consistent with a reading in which the fog is not an emanation of Chancery but the medium in which Chancery operates. If Dickens had written that the chimneys of the legal profession produced the fog, the chapter would be an allegory; as written, it is a description of a condition with an institution at its centre.” A satisfactory answer underlines the verbs; an excellent one notices that the law is described as producing documents, not fog.
depth.summary: Bleak House opens with an argument in the form of weather: present tense, anaphora, rival metaphors and a final contraction onto one room. The chapter establishes extent and centrality, and deliberately withholds a cause, which is why the fog can be read either as symbol or as obfuscation.

lessons.title: Interiority without a monitor: chapter XLII of The Portrait of a Lady
lessons.explanation: Chapter XLII of The Portrait of a Lady is the novel’s most discussed chapter and almost nothing happens in it. Isabel sits in a drawing room late at night and thinks. James signals the method in his first sentence, which begins after the event it reports: “She had answered nothing because his words had put the situation before her and she was absorbed in looking at it.” The tense is past perfect, so the reader enters a mind already occupied, and the chapter’s subject is announced as “the situation”, a word that implies a shape someone has to see. What follows is not a stream of consciousness but a sequence of hypotheses, each formulated, tested against remembered detail and then revised. She asks whether Lord Warburton still cares for her, answers that “there was something”, corrects herself, suspects Osmond of using her, then breaks out of what the narration calls a labyrinth: “Then she broke out of the labyrinth, rubbing her eyes, and declared that her imagination surely did her little honour and that her husband’s did him even less.” A chapter in which a woman sits still is therefore a chapter with a plot, and its events are inferences. Lesson 33 examined free indirect discourse as a way of putting a character’s judgement inside a narrator’s sentence; here the technique is extended over twenty pages, and the question becomes architectural rather than local.
lessons.example: The chapter’s central passage shows how James converts reflection into event. Isabel measures her marriage: “She had taken all the first steps in the purest confidence, and then she had suddenly found the infinite vista of a multiplied life to be a dark, narrow alley with a dead wall at the end.” The figure is hers in substance, since it revises the earlier imagery of a vista, but the sentence is the narrator’s, and the tidy antithesis of vista and alley is a writer’s arrangement rather than a thinker’s drift. The passage continues with a definition that has the air of a clinical report: “Suffering, with Isabel, was an active condition; it was not a chill, a stupor, a despair; it was a passion of thought, of speculation, of response to every pressure.” Three negations and a triad of nouns, and the effect is to make suffering sound like a faculty. Then comes the accusation and its careful limit: “She knew of no wrong he had done; he was not violent, he was not cruel: she simply believed he hated her. That was all she accused him of, and the miserable part of it was precisely that it was not a crime, for against a crime she might have found redress.” The vocabulary is legal, crime and redress, and it places the marriage in the same world as the Court of Chancery in Bleak House: a wrong that no court can hear. The chapter ends its movement with the house: “he had led her into the mansion of his own habitation, then, then she had seen where she really was”, and “It was the house of darkness, the house of dumbness, the house of suffocation.”
lessons.question: A student calls chapter XLII an interruption of the plot and proposes to summarise it in a sentence. What is the strongest reply?
lessons.answer: The chapter’s events are inferences: Isabel forms, tests and abandons readings of her husband and of Warburton, so summarising it as “she thinks about her marriage” removes the sequence that constitutes the chapter
lessons.distractor: The chapter is not an interruption because James wrote it, and an author’s decisions are by definition structural
lessons.correction: The intentionalist reply asserts structure without showing any. What makes the chapter an action is the visible revision of hypotheses, including her rejection of her own suspicion as unworthy, and the arrival at a formulation she had not held at the start, that her husband’s dislike is not a crime and therefore has no remedy. A summary that keeps “she thinks” and drops the revisions has kept the setting and discarded the plot.

depth.definitions: Interiority is the representation of a character’s mental life. Free indirect discourse reports a character’s thought in the narrator’s grammar, without quotation marks or a reporting clause. Hypotaxis is the arrangement of clauses in subordinate structures; parataxis sets them side by side. Retrospection is narration from a point after the events, often in the past perfect. Solidity of specification is James’s phrase in ‘The Art of Fiction’ for the concrete detail that produces the illusion of life. Prerequisites: lesson 33 on free indirect discourse, lesson 51 on scene and summary, and lesson 76 on the Dickens chapter that this one is compared with.
depth.mechanism: James makes thought do the work of action by four means. The chapter is framed as a single continuous occasion, a night in one room, which gives it the unity of a scene. Its tense is retrospective, so the reader learns what Isabel had already understood, which converts revelation into confirmation. Each hypothesis is stated, examined and replaced, and the replacements are marked by idioms of movement, breaking out of a labyrinth, rubbing her eyes, which gives thinking the shape of escape and return. And the metaphors escalate from architecture to confinement, vista, alley, wall, mansion, house, so that the chapter’s argument about the marriage is carried by a progression of images rather than by a proposition. The limitation is attribution: because the narrator supplies the sentences, the reader cannot treat every judgement as Isabel’s, and the chapter’s authority depends on a narrator whose sympathy is visible but whose agreement is not guaranteed.
depth.secondExample: Set the “house of darkness, the house of dumbness, the house of suffocation” beside Dickens’s “Fog everywhere” and the same figure can be seen doing opposite work. Dickens repeats a noun to widen: fog up the river, on the marshes, in the rigging, in the lungs, until the repetition has covered a city. James repeats a noun to narrow: darkness, dumbness, suffocation are three aspects of one interior, and the repetition closes a space rather than opening one. Both passages end in a building, and both use institutional vocabulary to describe a trap, Dickens through Chancery and James through crime and redress. The comparison is useful because it prevents a familiar mistake, which is to treat anaphora as inherently rhetorical in one direction. The device supplies emphasis; what the emphasis is for depends on whether the series expands or contracts, and that is a decision the reader can describe.
depth.mistake: Two errors recur. The first is the impatient one, that nothing happens in the chapter, which mistakes event for incident and ignores the revisions that constitute the chapter’s action. The second is the credulous one, that the chapter’s sentences are simply Isabel’s thoughts, which ignores the narratorial arrangement visible in the triads and the balanced clauses. Diagnose the second by asking whether a woman thinking at midnight would produce a sentence with three negations and a definition of suffering as “an active condition”; the answer is that she might feel it and would not phrase it so. A further error is to read the chapter as James’s endorsement of Isabel’s view of Osmond, when the novel has given her a history of misreading, and the chapter itself records one such misreading being corrected.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: list the hypotheses Isabel forms in chapter XLII in order, mark where each is accepted, qualified or abandoned, and then write 150 words on what the chapter’s plot is. Worked model, self-checked: “Hypothesis one: Warburton still cares for her. Evidence: her sense that the link is ‘as thin as a hair’ but audible. Qualified: she decides he may be sincere about Pansy. Hypothesis two: Osmond is using her to secure Pansy’s marriage. Accepted, then complicated by her refusal to think him duplicitous. Hypothesis three: her husband dislikes her. Accepted, with the crucial qualification that this is not a crime and gives her no redress. The plot is therefore a sequence of corrections ending in a formulation she can live with, which is why the chapter’s last movement turns to the house rather than to either man.” A satisfactory answer orders the hypotheses; an excellent one notices where she chooses not to know something.
depth.summary: Chapter XLII turns reflection into action: a night in one room, a retrospective tense, a series of hypotheses revised, and a chain of architectural metaphors that ends in a house of darkness. The sentences are the narrator’s, the judgements are Isabel’s, and the gap between them is where interpretation happens.

lessons.title: The ending as verdict: Tess, the black flag and the sentence Hardy had to defend
lessons.explanation: The last chapter of Tess of the d’Urbervilles approaches the execution through the eyes of people watching a building. The description is precise and administrative: a large red-brick structure with “rows of short barred windows bespeaking captivity”, an “ugly flat-topped octagonal tower”, a tall staff on the cornice. Then three short sentences: “Their eyes were riveted on it. A few minutes after the hour had struck something moved slowly up the staff, and extended itself upon the breeze. It was a black flag.” Only after that does the famous sentence arrive: “‘Justice’ was done, and the President of the Immortals, in Æschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess.” Four elements in one sentence, and each is doing something different. The word “Justice” is in quotation marks, which signals that the narrator is quoting a verdict rather than endorsing one. “Was done” is passive, so no executioner, judge or Home Secretary appears. “President of the Immortals” is a periphrasis, a title rather than a name, and “in Æschylean phrase” tags it as a borrowing from tragedy. “Had ended his sport” makes the killing a game whose player has finished. The next sentence completes the measurement: “And the d’Urberville knights and dames slept on in their tombs unknowing.” The ancestors who gave Tess her name are asleep and ignorant, and the word “unknowing” is the novel’s last judgement on the family romance that began the plot.
lessons.example: Take the sentence apart clause by clause and ask what each one refuses to say. The quotation marks around “Justice” refuse to let the law’s word stand as the narrator’s; they turn the state’s conclusion into reported speech. The passive “was done” refuses agency, which is the same grammatical move Gibbon uses to hide who acted, and here it produces the effect of a machine completing its cycle. The title “President of the Immortals” refuses the name God while keeping the attribute of sovereignty, so the sentence is theological without being doctrinal. The tag “in Æschylean phrase” refuses originality: the narrator is telling us that this way of speaking about human suffering comes from Greek tragedy, which is a literary pedigree rather than a personal creed. And “sport” refuses dignity to the proceeding, since a sport is what one does for amusement. Hardy was attacked for the sentence, and his 1892 postscript answers the attack in his own voice: one objector, he writes, “was a gentleman who turned Christian for half-an-hour the better to express his grief that a disrespectful phrase about the Immortals should have been used”. His defence is that the exclamation has precedent. He cites Gloucester in King Lear, “As flies to wanton boys are we to the gods; / They kill us for their sport”, and adds that “to exclaim illogically against the gods, singular or plural, is not such an original sin of mine as he seems to imagine.” The word “illogically” is the crucial admission: Hardy is defending the sentence’s right to be an exclamation, not claiming it as a proof.
lessons.question: A student writes that the final sentence expresses Hardy’s personal belief that the universe is indifferent and that the novel therefore teaches fatalism. What is the best correction?
lessons.answer: The sentence is marked as a quotation from tragic convention, and Hardy’s own defence treats it as an exclamation with literary precedent, so the novel’s attitude has to be argued from the whole ending rather than from the phrase alone
lessons.distractor: The sentence cannot express Hardy’s belief because novelists never speak in their own voices and every statement belongs to a narrator
lessons.correction: The general rule is too strong, since narrators often approximate their authors, and it would make the question unanswerable rather than answerable. The specific evidence is stronger: the quotation marks around “Justice”, the tag “in Æschylean phrase”, and Hardy’s postscript, which cites Shakespeare and Greek tragedy and calls the exclamation illogical. Those marks tell you what kind of sentence it is. What the novel believes remains a further question, to be settled by the black flag, the sleeping knights and the two figures who join hands and walk on.

depth.definitions: A periphrasis is a roundabout way of naming something, often a title in place of a name. Passive voice removes or demotes the agent of a verb. An allusion is an implicit or explicit reference to another text. A postscript in a novel’s front matter is an authorial note added after first publication. A verdict is a formal finding, and the quotation marks around “Justice” convert the word into a reported verdict. Prerequisites: lesson 60 on defending an interpretation against its strongest objection, lesson 72 on irony produced by grammar, and lesson 75 on endings that close a frame.
depth.mechanism: The sentence works by draining agency and then restoring it as theology. Passive voice removes the human executant; the periphrasis removes the divine name while keeping divine power; the genre tag removes originality by assigning the formula to tragedy; “sport” removes seriousness from the act. Four removals, and the result is a sentence in which nobody is responsible and everything is fated, which is precisely the condition the novel has spent five hundred pages showing to be a human production. That gap is the sentence’s critical force, and it is why the quotation marks matter: they signal that the fatalistic formula is available to the narrator as a way of describing what has happened, not as an explanation of why. What the sentence cannot do is deliver a doctrine: a reader cannot get from it alone to a creed, and Hardy’s postscript confirms that he expected readers to hear an exclamation rather than a proposition.
depth.secondExample: Hardy’s revisions show how directly an ending’s meaning depends on editorial decisions. He notes in the 1895 front matter that “The present edition of this novel contains a few pages that have never appeared in any previous edition”, adding that they were omitted when the episodes were collected though “they were in the original manuscript”, and that “They occur in Chapter X.” More consequentially for the ending, the Victorian Web essay by William Heffernan records that Hardy removed both the mock marriage and the drugging of Tess from the 1892 edition in order to restore what Hardy called “the true reading”, “seduction pure & simple”. The final sentence is unchanged by that revision, and its meaning is not. If Tess is drugged, the execution closes a story of assault; if she is seduced, it closes a story of ruin and blame, and the phrase “President of the Immortals” then reads as an indictment of a moral order rather than of a predator. The same words, two verdicts, and the difference is a documented editorial choice.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is to lift “President of the Immortals” out of the sentence and treat it as Hardy’s creed, which produces a novelist who wrote a treatise and called it a novel. Its mirror is to treat the phrase as mere ornament, an allusion with no bearing on the story’s judgement. The first is diagnosed by pointing to the quotation marks, the genre tag and the postscript’s word “illogically”; diagnose the second by pointing out that an ornament does not usually provoke pamphlets, and that Hardy wrote three dated notes defending his text. One more error is to ignore the edition, since the moral weight of the ending depends on whether the reader has the 1891, 1892 or later text in hand.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: rewrite the final paragraph as a newspaper report of an execution, keeping every verifiable fact and removing the figures. End with 150 words on what the fictional sentences add. Model response, self-reviewed: “The report reads: at eight o’clock a black flag was raised over the prison tower, indicating that the sentence had been carried out. The difference is not information but evaluation. The report has an agent, the prison, and a purpose, public notice. Hardy’s sentences have neither, and they substitute a title for a name and a game for a killing, so the reader is invited to see the execution as the completion of a contest rather than the act of a state. The last sentence about the sleeping knights adds the one thing a report cannot, which is the irrelevance of the family whose name caused the disaster.” A satisfactory answer keeps the facts straight; an excellent one notices that the report must name an authority that Hardy’s sentence removes.
depth.summary: Hardy’s last sentence is a machine for removing agency: quoted “Justice”, passive verb, divine periphrasis, tragic tag, and a word, “sport”, that empties the act of seriousness. Hardy defended it as an exclamation with precedent, and the novel’s attitude has to be argued from the whole ending and from the edition in hand.
