lessons.title: Disinterestedness and the tribunal: Arnold’s rule and Eliot’s reply
lessons.explanation: Arnold’s ‘The Function of Criticism at the Present Time’, collected in Essays in Criticism in 1865, gives criticism a single rule and a single aim. The aim is stated in words he is quoting from his own earlier preface on translating Homer: the endeavour “to see the object as in itself it really is”. The rule follows in a paragraph that refuses any practical test: criticism must keep “aloof from what is called ‘the practical view of things’”, and must follow “the law of its own nature, which is to be a free play of the mind on all subjects which it touches”. Arnold’s justification is that such play is “a pleasure in itself” and an “essential provider of elements without which a nation’s spirit ... must, in the long run, die of inanition”. He even remarks that the word curiosity, which in other languages names “this disinterested love of a free play of the mind on all subjects, for its own sake”, has in English “no sense but a rather bad and disparaging one”. The purpose of the essay is to defend a discipline that has no immediate use, and its method is to define that discipline by what it refuses. Lesson 58 examined the critic’s several jobs, review, scholarship and appreciation; this lesson takes the most influential attempt to give them a single norm, and then the most influential reply.
lessons.example: Arnold’s criterion can be tested on his own example. He praises Burke in a sentence that is itself a demonstration of the style he values: “But Burke is so great because, almost alone in England, he brings thought to bear upon politics, he saturates politics with thought.” The judgement is not that Burke was right about the French Revolution, and Arnold says explicitly that it was Burke’s misfortune that his ideas served “an epoch of concentration” rather than an epoch of expansion. Greatness is located in the relation between thought and subject, not in the conclusion. That is what disinterestedness means in practice, and it is a genuinely severe standard, because it forbids praising a writer for agreeing with you. Now notice the difficulty. If a critic fails to see the object as it is, how would a reader know? Arnold gives no procedure, no test case, no account of what counts as evidence for the relation he praises. His essay names a disposition and illustrates it; it does not specify a method. The strength of the position is that it blocks the reduction of criticism to politics or to utility. The weakness is that it cannot adjudicate between two critics who both claim to be disinterested and who describe the object differently, which is the situation in which readers actually need help.
lessons.question: Arnold writes that criticism must keep aloof from “the practical view of things” and follow “a free play of the mind”. What does this rule fail to supply?
lessons.answer: A procedure: the rule names a disposition but gives no test by which a reader could tell a disinterested reading from an interested one that claims to be disinterested
lessons.distractor: A subject matter, since the rule forbids criticism from discussing politics and so leaves criticism with nothing to write about
lessons.correction: The rule does not forbid political subjects; Arnold discusses the French Revolution at length and praises Burke for saturating politics with thought. What it forbids is assessing a work by its practical consequences. The missing element is procedural, not topical: two critics may both claim to see the object as it is, and Arnold’s essay gives no way to decide between them, which is why Eliot’s reply turns on the question of who judges.

depth.definitions: Disinterestedness is the disposition of judging without regard to practical or partisan advantage; it is not the same as indifference, since it requires intense interest in the object. An epoch of concentration is Arnold’s term for a period dominated by practical conflict, as against an epoch of expansion in which ideas circulate freely. The inner voice, in Eliot’s essay, is the doctrine that the writer should trust an inward authority rather than rules or tradition. A tribunal is a body with authority to decide. Prerequisites: lesson 58 on the critic’s job, lesson 67 on making the adverse case, and lesson 71 on Johnson’s appeal from criticism to nature, which is the third position compared below.
depth.mechanism: The two essays relocate the standard of judgement. Arnold locates it in the relation between a critic and an object: the critic must see the thing as it is, and the norm is a kind of perceptual fidelity. Eliot locates it in a relation among critics: criticism “must always profess an end in view”, namely “the elucidation of works of art and the correction of taste”, and the critic should “compose his differences with as many of his fellows as possible, in the common pursuit of true judgment”. This is an intersubjective standard, and it answers Arnold’s problem by supplying the missing tribunal. It creates a new problem, since competence is identified by the judgments it produces, so the tribunal risks circularity: the critics who agree define the competence by which agreement is measured. Eliot also does something subtler, which is to distinguish refutation from reception, writing of Arnold’s judgement on the Romantics that it “has not, so far as I know, ever been successfully controverted; and it has not, so far as I know, ever made very much impression on popular opinion”. That sentence is a model for any student: being right and being heard are different achievements, and an argument should not claim the second as evidence of the first.
depth.secondExample: Johnson supplies a third position, and the comparison is clarifying. Where Johnson writes of “an appeal open from criticism to nature” (lesson 71), Arnold writes of seeing the object as it is, and Eliot writes of the common pursuit of true judgment. Nature, the object, and the community of judges: three places to put the standard. Each can be asked the same question, which is what would show it failing. Johnson’s standard fails when “nature” turns out to be whatever the critic already believes about humanity, as when he convicts the metaphysicals for not pleasing the reader he has defined. Arnold’s fails when two disinterested readings conflict and neither can be shown to have seen the object better, which is most of the time. Eliot’s fails when the competent judges exclude a work that later readers accept, which is a historical event that can actually be documented, and which is why his position is the easiest of the three to test and the hardest to defend without qualification.
depth.mistake: The usual error is to paraphrase the two positions into slogans: Arnold says critics should be objective, Eliot says they should respect tradition. Both slogans lose the mechanism. Arnold’s rule is about the critic’s relation to the object and about the social value of free enquiry, not about neutrality of tone; Eliot’s is about the location of authority in a community of judges, not about deference to the past, and his essay is largely an attack on a doctrine of inward authority which he calls, with deliberate rudeness, Whiggery. A second error, common in examinations, is to call Eliot’s essay a refutation. It is a redescription: he accepts Arnold’s aim and disputes where judgement is seated, and the disagreement is more interesting, and more arguable, in that form.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take any review of a novel or a poem, from a newspaper or a journal, and mark every sentence in which it appeals to a standard. Classify each appeal as Johnsonian, which invokes nature or lasting human interest, Arnoldian, which invokes seeing the object truly or the value of free enquiry, or Eliotean, which invokes the judgment of competent readers or the tradition. Then add 150 words on what evidence would show the review failing by the standard it invokes most often. A model response, checked against the criteria: “The review appeals mostly to Eliotean competence, since it grounds its judgement on what ‘any serious reader’ will find. The evidence that would show it failing is documentary: a substantial body of competent readers, at the time and later, who found the opposite, which is exactly the kind of evidence Eliot’s standard makes relevant. Had the review appealed to Arnoldian disinterestedness, no comparable evidence would exist, and the review would be unfalsifiable in practice.” A satisfactory answer classifies the appeals; an excellent one notes which classification makes the review testable.
depth.summary: Arnold gives criticism a norm without a tribunal; Eliot supplies a tribunal without a criterion; Johnson supplies a standard outside both. The comparative question is always what would show the standard failing, and Eliot’s distinction between refutation and reception is the model of argumentative honesty the lesson leaves with the reader.

visual.title: Three places to put the standard: nature, the object, the community
visual.description: A three-column diagram comparing Johnson, Arnold and Eliot on where critical authority is located, with a bottom row giving the test that would show each standard failing.
steps: Column 1, Johnson: authority in nature, “an appeal open from criticism to nature”; failure test, when “nature” turns out to be the critic’s own preferences

Column 2, Arnold: authority in the critic’s relation to the object, “to see the object as in itself it really is” and “disinterestedness”; failure test, two disinterested readings that conflict with no way to decide

Column 3, Eliot: authority in a community, “the elucidation of works of art and the correction of taste” and “the common pursuit of true judgment”; failure test, competent judges excluding a work later accepted
Cross-arrow, Eliot on Arnold: the distinction between a judgement “never successfully controverted” and one that has made little “impression on popular opinion”
Cost box: Arnold lacks a tribunal, Eliot risks circularity in defining competence, Johnson lacks an operational definition
Payoff box: each supplies what the others lack, which is why the comparison is an argument rather than a scoreboard

lessons.title: Capstone: your own case about a prose passage, with its strongest objection and a test
lessons.explanation: Lesson 70 set out the shape of a defensible comparative case: a claim, a stated ground of comparison, the strongest adverse case, and a test that could fail. This lesson transfers that shape from poems to prose, where the temptation is greater because prose looks like ordinary language and readers therefore describe it impressionistically. The transfer requires one addition. In verse, the formal facts are visible on the page, since lines, stresses and rhymes can be counted. In prose the formal facts must be constructed by the reader, and the only honest way to do it is to count before interpreting: sentence lengths, the number of subordinate clauses, the number of clauses beginning with the same word, the ratio of nouns to verbs, the domains from which the metaphors are drawn. A claim that begins “Dickens’s style is dense” is unfalsifiable. A claim that begins “in the first chapter of Bleak House, eleven clauses open with the word Fog” is a fact, and a fact can be connected to an effect by an argument that someone else can check. The capstone is therefore a small piece of research with a written result, not an essay of appreciation.
lessons.example: Here is the method worked on a comparison that the previous lessons have prepared. Take two openings: the preface to Vanity Fair, where a manager watches a fair, and chapter I of Bleak House, where fog covers a city. Both are present tense, both are set pieces, and both end by concentrating attention on an institution, a theatre in the one case and the Court of Chancery in the other. The variable to isolate is the frame. Thackeray supplies a speaker who announces that what follows is a performance; Dickens supplies no speaker at all. Now state a claim with a mechanism: because Thackeray’s speaker is inside the fiction and admits to being one of the fair’s quacks, judgement in his novel is dramatised as a performance and the reader is invited to judge the judge, whereas Dickens’s absent speaker makes the chapter’s judgements look like facts about London, so the reader must reconstruct the evaluating voice from syntax alone. The strongest objection is that the difference is generic rather than designed: a preface is a place for a persona and a first chapter is a place for description, so the comparison measures the conventions of two paratextual slots. The test follows from the objection. If the difference is generic, then Dickens’s narration elsewhere should acquire a visible persona whenever he writes a preface, and Thackeray’s chapter one should drop the managerial voice once the performance has begun. Both predictions are checkable, and the second is the more interesting, since the narrator of Vanity Fair returns in his own person throughout the novel, which weakens the generic explanation and strengthens the claim that the frame is a device rather than a slot.
lessons.question: A student’s capstone claims that a passage’s long sentences create a feeling of entrapment, and offers three quotations containing long sentences. What is missing?
lessons.answer: A contrast case and a stated mechanism: the essay needs a passage by the same author with short sentences, or an account of how length produces entrapment rather than, say, dignity or inertia, so that the claim predicts something checkable
lessons.distractor: More quotations, since three examples of a feature are not enough to establish that the feature is present throughout the text
lessons.correction: Quantity is not the weakness. Three quotations may be ample evidence that long sentences occur; what they cannot do is show that length is doing the work attributed to it, because dignity, ceremony, inertia and entrapment are all available effects of the same feature. The missing elements are a mechanism that selects one effect and a contrast that would show the effect disappearing when the feature does.

depth.definitions: A thesis is the claim the essay argues for. A mechanism is the account of how a feature produces an effect. An adverse case is the strongest available objection, stated in a form its holder would accept. A falsification test is a prediction which, if it failed, would count against the thesis. A contrast passage is a passage that differs in the feature under discussion while remaining comparable in author, genre or occasion. Prerequisites: lesson 70, whose method this lesson transfers, lesson 50 on thesis and counterargument, and lessons 71 to 79, which supply the passages and the vocabulary.
depth.mechanism: The capstone works by converting an impression into a prediction. Counting produces the fact; the mechanism connects the fact to an effect by a stated route, such as the reader’s inability to locate a judging voice; the adverse case attacks the mechanism rather than the fact, since rival explanations of the same fact are the real threat; and the test is derived from the adverse case, so that answering the objection and testing the thesis are the same operation. This is the difference between a research essay and a display of reading. The price of the method is that prose offers fewer hard facts than verse, so the counts must be described precisely enough for another reader to reproduce them, and the edition must be named, since punctuation, paragraphing and even wording vary between witnesses, as the Bleak House transcription variants show.
depth.secondExample: A second specimen uses the technique of lesson 77. James’s chapter XLII repeats a noun frame three times, “the house of darkness, the house of dumbness, the house of suffocation”, where Dickens repeats “Fog” across a paragraph. The fact is a shared figure; the claim is that James’s triad contracts a space while Dickens’s anaphora expands one. Mechanism: in Dickens the repeated noun takes a new prepositional complement each time, so each repetition adds territory; in James the repeated noun keeps the same genitive frame and changes only the abstract noun, so each repetition adds an aspect of one condition. The adverse case is that the difference is one of subject matter, since a city invites a survey and a marriage invites an interior. The test: find a passage where James surveys an exterior, such as the opening description of Gardencourt, and see whether his syntax expands or contracts there. If James’s exterior description also contracts, the subject-matter explanation fails and the stylistic one holds. That is a test a reader can actually run, which is the only kind worth proposing.
depth.mistake: Three errors ruin capstones. The evidence pile adds quotations of the same kind, which increases the sample without discriminating. The straw objection states a rival so weak that refuting it is easy, usually by attributing to opponents a claim no serious reader holds. The unfalsifiable test proposes a check that the thesis would survive whatever the result, as when a student promises to look for further instances of the feature already found. Diagnose each by asking a single question of the finished draft: what result would make me abandon this thesis? If no result would, the essay is a statement of taste with quotations attached, and the remedy is to name the result first and then argue.
depth.application: Nonblocking task, the capstone proper: choose a passage of 200 to 300 words from any text in this level, transcribe it from a named edition, and write a case of roughly 600 words in six numbered parts. One, the passage and its edition. Two, the formal description, with counts. Three, the thesis and its mechanism. Four, the strongest adverse case, stated fairly. Five, the test, with its predicted result. Six, the reply to the objection. Model opening, self-reviewed: “The passage is the second paragraph of chapter I of Bleak House, transcribed from the Project Gutenberg text of 1023. It contains eleven clauses opening with Fog, and their complements move from river to marsh to shipping to bodies. My thesis is that the sequence is an inventory whose order is an argument about distribution, and that the chapter’s final contraction onto Lincoln’s Inn Hall depends on the reader having been taken through the whole list. The strongest objection is that the list is a convention of topographical writing and carries no argument. The test is a comparison with the same novel’s description of Chesney Wold, where the weather is also present and no institution is at the centre; if the inventory there produces no contraction, the claim that the order is argumentative survives.” A satisfactory case has all six parts; an excellent one names a result that would defeat it.
depth.summary: A prose case is built in six parts: a transcribed passage with its edition, a counted description, a thesis with a mechanism, the strongest adverse case, a test derived from that objection, and a reply. The question that separates research from appreciation is what result would make the writer give the thesis up.

visual.title: Six stages from passage to tested case
visual.description: A flow diagram of the capstone method as six boxes in sequence, with a return arrow from the test to the thesis labelled “revise or abandon”.
steps: Stage 1, passage and edition: 200 to 300 words, transcribed, with the witness named, since punctuation and wording vary
Stage 2, counted description: clause openings, subordination, sentence lengths, metaphor domains, person and tense
Stage 3, thesis and mechanism: a claim that connects one counted feature to one effect by a stated route
Stage 4, adverse case: the strongest rival explanation, such as genre convention, authorial intention or subject matter
Stage 5, test: a contrast passage or an earlier edition, with a predicted result derived from the objection
Stage 6, reply: what the result showed, and what would still count against the thesis
Return arrow: from stage 5 back to stage 3, labelled “revise or abandon”, which is the mark of a case rather than a display

questions.prompt: A student argues that the fog in Bleak House “symbolises the Court of Chancery” and offers the anaphora of “Fog everywhere” as proof that Dickens means the fog to stand for the law. A tutor asks for the difference between the two claims. Which formulation is most accurate?
questions.answer: The anaphora establishes that the fog is pervasive and that the chapter’s syntax is organised by it; the symbolic equivalence with Chancery is an interpretation supported by the chapter’s closing movement towards Lincoln’s Inn Hall, not by the repetition alone
questions.distractor: The two claims are identical, because a repeated image in a nineteenth-century novel is by definition a symbol
questions.correction: Repetition establishes prominence, not reference. What the chapter does verifiably is widen the fog from river to marsh to ships to lungs and then contract it to one building, so the final clause makes Chancery the centre of a condition rather than its cause. The symbolic reading is defensible, but it has to be argued from that structure and from the chapter’s own metaphors, such as mud accumulating “at compound interest”.

questions.prompt: Chapter XLII of The Portrait of a Lady reports a woman sitting alone and thinking for most of its length. A student calls it an interruption of the plot and proposes skipping it. Which reply is best grounded in the chapter’s text?
questions.answer: The chapter’s action is inference: Isabel tests and revises readings of her husband and of Lord Warburton, and the chapter’s metaphors, ending in the house “of darkness, of dumbness, of suffocation”, are the novel’s account of what her marriage is
questions.distractor: The chapter is skippable because nothing changes in it, and a novel’s argument is carried by events rather than by reflection
questions.correction: Something does change: she moves from not having asked herself a question to having answered it, and she abandons one hypothesis for another within the chapter. The claim that reflection is not action is a thesis about novels, not an observation about this one, and it is contradicted by a chapter whose plot is the correction of a misreading, which is the same operation the reader performs on the novel.

questions.prompt: A student writes that the last sentence of Tess of the d’Urbervilles states Hardy’s own view that the universe is indifferent, and that the novel therefore teaches fatalism. Hardy’s 1892 postscript is cited in objection. What does the postscript actually show?
questions.answer: Hardy treats the phrase as a literary allusion with a pedigree, defending it by citing Gloucester in King Lear, which makes the sentence a quoted tragic formula rather than a confession of the author’s creed
questions.distractor: The postscript shows that Hardy was a Christian who accepted providence and wrote the phrase under editorial pressure
questions.correction: Hardy’s defence is literary, not doctrinal: he answers the charge of disrespect by pointing out that the exclamation has precedent, in Shakespeare and in the Greek tragedians, and he mocks the objector as a gentleman who “turned Christian for half-an-hour”. That is a defence of the phrase’s register, and it leaves open what the novel believes. Reading the sentence as a creed converts a cited formula into a doctrine and skips the quotation marks around “Justice”.

questions.prompt: A seminar reports that Eliot “refuted” Arnold’s rule of disinterestedness in 1923 because Eliot denied that criticism could be detached from tradition and belief. Which assessment of that report is most accurate?
questions.answer: Eliot replaced a standard with a tribunal: he kept the demand for judgment but located it in the common pursuit of true judgment by competent critics, which answers Arnold’s lack of an enforcing body while raising the question of who counts as competent
questions.distractor: Eliot refuted Arnold because he showed that disinterestedness is impossible, and a refutation of a norm’s feasibility ends the argument
questions.correction: Showing that a norm is hard to meet is not refuting it, and Eliot does not claim impossibility; he claims that criticism is a cooperative discipline with a tradition. The instructive contrast is structural: Arnold supplies a criterion with no tribunal, Eliot a tribunal with no criterion, and each supplies what the other lacks. Calling this a refutation flattens a disagreement about where judgement is seated into a victory.

questions.prompt: A final essay offers a thesis about Dickens’s syntax, three quotations that support it, and a paragraph summarising the plot of Bleak House. The marker writes “no adverse case, no test”. What would repair the essay most directly?
questions.answer: Name the strongest rival explanation, such as genre convention or a compositor’s punctuation, and specify a comparison passage where the same feature is absent, so the thesis predicts a difference a reader could check
questions.distractor: Add a fourth and fifth quotation from the same chapter, since more evidence of the same kind answers an objection
questions.correction: Additional quotations of the same kind increase the sample but not the discrimination: they cannot show that the feature is distinctive to this author or this passage. Lesson 70 established the comparative test for poems, and it transfers unchanged: the objection must be stated in its strongest form and the thesis must say what would count against it, which requires a contrast case rather than more of the same evidence.

questions.prompt: Two novelists open with present-tense set pieces. Thackeray’s “Before the Curtain” places a named manager before a fair and lets him comment; Dickens opens Bleak House with mud, smoke and fog and no narrator visible at all until the chapter’s final movement. A student claims the second opening is therefore more objective. Which assessment of that claim is best?
questions.answer: The absence of a visible speaker is itself a rhetorical choice: the chapter’s anaphora and its closing contraction onto Lincoln’s Inn Hall arrange the reader’s judgement as surely as Thackeray’s manager does, and objectivity is not established by invisibility
questions.distractor: The claim is sound, because a passage with no first-person pronoun reports rather than evaluates, and evaluation requires an explicit speaker
questions.correction: Evaluation can be carried by selection, by syntax and by metaphor without a pronoun. Dickens’s mud accumulates “at compound interest”, which is a judgement in the form of a figure, and the paragraph moves from river to marsh to ships to lungs before settling on one building. Thackeray makes the judging voice audible; Dickens makes it structural. The useful comparison is between two ways of installing a judge, not between presence and absence of judgement.

questions.prompt: Johnson writes in the Preface to Shakespeare that “Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature”, and in the Life of Cowley that the metaphysical poets’ reader “sometimes admires, is seldom pleased”. A student treats the second sentence as a change of standard. What does the repetition of the word “please” establish?
questions.answer: One criterion is being applied twice: durability of pleasure is Johnson’s test of poetry, and the metaphysicals fail it by astonishing rather than pleasing, so the two judgements are consistent applications of a single standard
questions.distractor: The word is used loosely in both places, since Johnson wrote the Life of Cowley fifteen years later and his opinions had shifted
questions.correction: The dates permit a shift but the wording records a continuity: “please long” in the Preface and “seldom pleased” in the Life name the same test, and the Life explains the failure mechanically, through wit that yokes heterogeneous ideas “by violence”. Reading the second sentence as a new standard misses the strongest feature of Johnson’s criticism, which is that a single criterion is turned against a poet he admires and a school he does not.

questions.prompt: The Gutenberg text of Gibbon’s first volume prints, at the foot of chapter XV, an editor’s note by Dean Milman which says that “the art of Gibbon” consists in “confounding together, in one undistinguishable mass, the origin and apostolic propagation of the Christian religion with its later progress”. A student quotes that note as Gibbon’s own admission. What is wrong, and what does the note actually offer?
questions.answer: The note is a nineteenth-century editor’s hostile reading printed on the same page, so it is evidence of how Gibbon was read, not of what Gibbon conceded; as a reading it is usable if it is attributed and tested against the chapter’s own sentences
questions.distractor: The note is worthless because an editor’s opinion is not part of the text and cannot be cited in an essay
questions.correction: Two errors are possible and the student makes the first: attribution. The note is Milman’s, marked with his initial in this edition, and it accuses Gibbon of a procedure rather than reporting a confession. The second error would be to discard it. Reception evidence is exactly what a reader of an ironic text needs, because it shows a contemporary-trained reader detecting the irony and resenting it, which is stronger support for the ironic reading than the student’s own intuition.

questions.prompt: Paine opens Crisis No. I with “THESE are the times that try men’s souls” and, according to the editor’s preface in the Conway edition, the last Crisis of 1783 “opens with the words, ‘The times that tried men’s souls are over.’” A student reads the later sentence as Paine contradicting himself. Which reading of the pair is best?
questions.answer: The later sentence reuses a formula that had become public property, converting a present-tense summons into a retrospective marker, which shows the phrase working as an instrument rather than as a proposition to be contradicted
questions.distractor: The later sentence contradicts the earlier one, since a time of trial cannot both be present and be over
questions.correction: The two sentences are uttered eight years apart about different moments, so there is no contradiction to find. What the pair demonstrates is the portability of a designed formula: the first sentence addresses a crisis in progress and the second closes it by echoing the opening, a technique of return rather than of assertion. Reading pamphlets as though they were timeless arguments rather than dated interventions produces exactly this false contradiction.

questions.prompt: Hazlitt objects to Johnson’s style on the ground that “there is no discrimination, no selection, no variety in it”, while Johnson’s own Preface argues that lasting writing depends on “just representations of general nature”. A student proposes to settle the dispute by counting. Which version of that test would actually discriminate?
questions.answer: Compare Johnson’s parallel clauses with Hazlitt’s in a passage of the same length and genre, and ask whether the balance in each case registers a distinction or merely repeats a shape, since the dispute is about whether the figure carries thought
questions.distractor: Count the words of Latin origin in each writer, since Hazlitt’s charge is that Johnson preferred long Latin words to common English ones
questions.correction: Etymology measures vocabulary, and Hazlitt’s charge is about selection and discrimination, which is a claim about whether the second half of a clause adds a distinction. The Latin count tests a different accusation, the one about “tall, opaque words”. The discriminating test is functional: take matched passages, mark the antitheses, and ask of each pair whether the second term narrows, corrects or merely restates the first.

questions.prompt: Thackeray’s novel opens with a manager looking into the fair and closes with the instruction “come, children, let us shut up the box and the puppets, for our play is played out”. A student argues that the closing return proves the frame was decorative, since the story would stand without it. Which reply is strongest?
questions.answer: The return is what makes the frame a device rather than a preface: it fixes the novel’s duration as a performance and makes the reader, addressed as “children”, the audience whose judgement the manager has been soliciting throughout
questions.distractor: The return proves the opposite of what the student says, because any repetition in a novel is structural and therefore meaningful
questions.correction: The second reply would be a slogan, not an argument. What supports the first is the change in address: the opening speaks of the manager in the third person, slides into “I take it”, and the close speaks directly to “children”. The repetition matters because the addressee has shifted and the metaphor has been given a terminus. A frame that opens and shuts a box is a claim about the status of the characters, which is why an abridgement that removes either end alters the novel’s argument.

questions.prompt: Dickens writes that the mud is “accumulating at compound interest”, that the shops’ gas has “a haggard and unwilling look”, and that the fog reaches “the eyes and throats of ancient Greenwich pensioners”. A student concludes that the passage personifies the weather. Which account of the figures is most accurate, and most useful for an argument?
questions.answer: The figures are mixed in kind and each carries a different claim: the financial metaphor makes the city a debtor, the gas attributed a mood registers exhaustion, and the fog in lungs converts a landscape into a public-health fact
questions.distractor: All three are personification, and identifying the trope is sufficient analysis of the passage
questions.correction: Labelling all three personification loses the distinction that does the interpretive work. Compound interest is a metaphor from finance, the haggard gas is a projection of feeling, and fog in the throat is literal physiology offered as evidence. A reader who stops at the trope’s name has classified the passage without saying what any figure claims, which is the difference between identifying a device and reading it.

questions.prompt: In chapter XLII of The Portrait of a Lady the narration reports that Isabel’s suffering “was a passion of thought, of speculation, of response to every pressure”, and that Osmond had led her “into the mansion of his own habitation”, which becomes “the house of darkness, the house of dumbness, the house of suffocation”. A student asks whether these are Isabel’s words or the narrator’s. What is the best answer, and what follows for interpretation?
questions.answer: The syntax is the narrator’s and the judgement is hers: the triadic anaphora and the tight subordination belong to the reporting voice, while the metaphors extend her earlier image of the “dead wall”, so the passage fuses her figure with his sentence
questions.distractor: The words must be Isabel’s, because the chapter stays inside her consciousness and a narrator cannot know what a house feels like to inhabit
questions.correction: Access and attribution are different questions, and this is the error the student is making. A narrator who reports a character’s thoughts may still choose the words, and the choice is visible in the formal pattern: three noun phrases with the same frame, a rhythm no character is shown composing. The consequence is that the novel’s account of the marriage is neither a neutral report nor a quotation but an interpretation the reader is invited to test against her earlier metaphors.

questions.prompt: Hardy writes that “‘Justice’ was done, and the President of the Immortals, in Æschylean phrase, had ended his sport with Tess”, and in his 1892 postscript he answers a critic by quoting Gloucester in King Lear: “As flies to wanton boys are we to the gods; / They kill us for their sport.” A student says the postscript proves the sentence is Hardy’s own view. What does the evidence actually support?
questions.answer: It supports a claim about register and precedent: Hardy defends the phrase as a citation of tragic convention, which tells us what kind of sentence it is, while the question of what the novel believes remains to be argued from the ending’s other details
questions.distractor: It supports the student, because an author who defends a sentence in his own voice must agree with everything the sentence says
questions.correction: Defending a sentence’s right to exist is not endorsing its proposition. Hardy’s defence is that the exclamation has authority behind it in Shakespeare and in Greek tragedy, and he is answering a charge of disrespect rather than a charge of atheism. Meanwhile the quotation marks around “Justice” and the passive “was done” do their own work, and any account of the novel’s belief has to reckon with them rather than with the postscript alone.

questions.prompt: Arnold writes that criticism must aim “to see the object as in itself it really is” and sums up its rule as “disinterestedness”; Eliot replies that criticism “must always profess an end in view” and that the critic should compose his differences with others “in the common pursuit of true judgment”. A student asks which of the two positions is falsifiable. Which answer is best?
questions.answer: Eliot’s, in principle: a tribunal of competent readers can be shown to have excluded a work later accepted, whereas Arnold’s rule names no procedure whose failure could be detected
questions.distractor: Neither is falsifiable, so the choice between them is merely temperamental and no argument is possible
questions.correction: The second answer gives up too quickly. Arnold’s norm is a disposition with no specified test, which is a real weakness, but Eliot’s tribunal has its own circularity: competence is identified by the judgments it produces. The productive comparison is that each supplies what the other lacks, a criterion without an institution and an institution without a criterion, and a reader who states both weaknesses has the makings of an argument rather than a verdict.

questions.prompt: An essay argues that Bleak House’s opening “shows Dickens’s belief that the legal system causes all the misery of London”, and supports it with the chapter’s closing sentence about the Lord Chancellor sitting “at the very heart of the fog”. A marker objects that the quotation supports a weaker claim than the one asserted. What is the gap?
questions.answer: The sentence places Chancery at the centre of the fog, which is a claim about where the condition concentrates, not about what produces it, so causality needs further evidence from the chapter’s other figures and from the novel’s plot
questions.distractor: The quotation is irrelevant because the chapter is description and description cannot make causal claims
questions.correction: Description can carry causal claims, which is why the objection is not that the evidence is the wrong kind but that it is too weak for the thesis. Centre is not cause: the chapter’s mud and smoke have other sources, and a Victorian Web reading of the same imagery argues that Dickens deliberately leaves the fog’s origins unidentified. The essay should either narrow its thesis to centrality or gather evidence that attributes production, which is the discipline lesson 40 sets out for symbols.

questions.prompt: A student’s capstone argues that Hazlitt’s familiar style is more honest than Johnson’s balanced prose, quoting “I like to go by myself” and Johnson’s “Nothing can please many, and please long”. The student’s only engagement with objection is the sentence “Some readers prefer Johnson”. Which revision turns this into a real case?
questions.answer: Restate the objection as the strongest available claim (that balance is itself a form of precision, as Johnson’s distinction between pleasing and astonishing suggests), then name a comparison passage where Hazlitt’s plainness fails to discriminate, so the thesis predicts a difference that could be checked
questions.distractor: Add the observation that Johnson was a Tory and Hazlitt a radical, since political allegiance explains stylistic preference and settles the question
questions.correction: The political explanation replaces the argument with a cause, and it does not tell the reader which prose is more honest. The objection as given is a preference, not a case, which is exactly what lesson 70 warned against. A real case states the rival claim in a form its holder would accept and then produces a test: a passage where the favoured style loses the distinction it claims to secure. Without that, the essay has a thesis and no risk.
